item.title: The Story Behind the Name ‘Blade Runner’ Has Nothing to Do With Replicants
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail

Ridley Scottâs Blade Runner opens in 1982 with a scrolling text about outlawed androids and the âBlade Runner Unitsâ sent to shoot them on sight.

âI think âexplanationsâ are the bug-bears of screenplay writing and I like to stay clear of them,â screenwriter Hampton Fancher told Vulture in 2017. The source novel wonât help either: Rick Deckard is a plain old bounty hunter in Dickâs Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968), and blade runner is, as one literature professorâs study guide puts it, âa term which occurs nowhere in the book.â

The story starts in a doctorâs office.

The Doctorâs Smugglers

Alan E. Nourse practiced medicine in Washington state after getting his medical degree from the University of Pennsylvania in 1955, and he wrote science fiction on the side until 1963, when he retired from medicine to write full-time, according to Josephine Riesmanâs history of the title.

In 1974, he published a novel called The Bladerunner. Itâs set in a future where health care is free to those the government deems fit, but the price of treatment is sterilization. Those who are ineligible have to go to black-market doctors, and the couriers who smuggle instruments to those doctors are the bladerunners: âunderground medical supply smugglers who assist black market doctors in providing health care for the ineligible,â as Cornell University Libraryâs exhibit on the novel and the film puts it.

Kirkus reviewed it that fall and described the hero, Billy Gimp, as Docâs âmedical supplier.â

Enter William S. Burroughs

Burroughs got hold of a copy around the end of 1976, and on December 5, his assistant James Grauerholz wrote to Burroughsâs agent that the author had âliked the book very much, and in fact has begun to consider a film treatment for it,â per Vulture.

Burroughs had the treatment done by March 1977 and called it The Blade Runner, splitting Nourseâs one word into two. Itâs pure Burroughs: written as a long explanation of the movie to someone named âB.J.,â packed with a civil war in greater New York and a black market in sperm, and ending with Billy realizing heâs been living in 1914 the whole time.

The film rights were given up after nobody showed any interest in making it. The treatment was later published as a book by Blue Wind Press in 1979, retitled Blade Runner (a movie) to keep it distinct from Nourseâs novel, which is a funny title for a movie nobody was making.

Fancherâs Bookshelf

At the time, Fancher was working on a script of Dickâs novel under working titles like Android, Mechanismo, and Dangerous Days. A few months in, Scott asked him what Deckard actually was and what he should be called, and Fancher didnât know.

âThat night, I was looking through my books and came across a thin little volume by William Burroughs called Blade Runner,â he told Vulture. âBingo! Everybody liked it, then later, we needed a new title other than the ones weâd been considering and Michael Deeley, the producer, said, âItâs staring us right in the face.ââ

According to Scott, the production then approached Burroughs and bought the title for âa nominal fee,â and the end credits of the film thank Burroughs and Nourse âfor the use of the title Blade Runner.â Nothing else of Nourseâs novel made it into the film: no scalpels, no smugglers, no sterilization laws, just the job title for a cop who hunts replicants.

Burroughsâs book did eventually end up in a movie, albeit a strange one. Tom Huckabee, one of its directors, folded it into the 1983 film Taking Tiger Mountain, starring a young Bill Paxton, and according to the Austin Chronicle, he paid $100 for the rights. So Ridley Scott got the title, and Bill Paxton got everything else.

The latest entry in the Blade Runner franchise, a series called Blade Runner 2099, is now streaming on Prime Video.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-28 01:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Most Popular Christmas Song the Year You Were Born
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context for an English learner

Some say fruitcake gets better with age, though most would agree the only Christmas treat that actually improves over time is of the audio, not edible, variety. After all, the right song can turn a humdrum December night into a holiday movie.

While the most classic of Christmas songs, from Bing Crosby's "White Christmas" to Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," transcend generational music tastes, their first or most prominent years on the charts as holiday hits help to define Christmases of the last century through what otherwise can be a sea of white and twinkling lights.

Holiday hits have evolved in a big way, from radio classics in the 1940s to R&B-pop remakes of the modern day. The 1950s and '60s gave us plenty of cozy staples still looped in every department store (you can thank this era for "Santa Baby" and "Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree"), while the '80s brought synth-pop hits like "Last Christmas" by Wham! that gave the season a very different sound. By the time '90s and 2000s babies arrived, Christmas playlists featured a mix of nostalgic and catchy new tunes destined to climb the charts in the new millennium.

So, which holiday hit topped the charts the year you ended up under the tree? To find out, we rounded up the biggest Christmas song for every year from 1940 to 2005, factoring in notable new holiday releases alongside Playback.fm's picksâwhich draw on "historical holiday and other popular chart and music data"âand Billboard holiday charts.

Whether your family strictly sticks to the Christmas classics anchored by Crosby or puts a Gen Z twist on the playlist with a bit of Bieber, does the festive favorite from your birth year still track? Or should the top Christmas song from the year you were born stay in the holiday past?

item.title: The Best Ben Stiller Comedies, Ranked by Rotten Tomatoes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: moderate learning value, not as focused on original reporting

In the late '90s and early 2000s, Ben Stiller was a household name and king of comedy. It seemed like everyone could quote lines from at least one of his films. He could have the audience in stitches no matter the role he played, protagonist or antagonist. But in 2017, Stiller stepped away from the limelight to focus on his family and to try his hand behind the camera.

Though not starring in many films anymore, Stiller does still act occasionally. His latest film, Focker-in-Law, is the fourth in the Meet the Parents series and is coming to theaters on November 25, 2026. Stiller stars alongside Robert De Niro and Ariana Grande, while also producing the film.

In honor of his return to the screen, we're looking at a few of Stiller's best comedies, according to Rotten Tomatoes.

Dodgeball: A True Underdog Story (2004) â 71%

If we had a nickel for every time Ben Stiller played a fat-phobic, fitness-crazed villain, we'd have two nickels. That isn't a lot, but it's weird that it happened twice. Stiller even said that his character, White Goodman in Dodgeball, was related to Tony Perkis, his character in Heavyweights. Whether that's true remains to be confirmed, but it is true that Goodman is one of Stiller's most popular roles. His over-the-top acting gives Dodgeball some of its best laughs and complements Vaughn's straight man, Peter La Fleur, perfectly.

The Royal Tenenbaums (2001) â 81%

If you had never seen The Royal Tenenbaums and just read a plot summary, you would not think it could be a comedy. The comic aspects come from the absurdity of what would normally be very serious matters. Ben Stiller's Chas Tenenbaum has lost his wife and is now a single parent of two boys. His dysfunctional family only adds more stress as his father (Gene Hackman) fakes cancer to renew relationships with his adult children. Stiller pulls off the emotional moments as well as the absurdist comedy.

Tropic Thunder (2008) â 82%

Tropic Thunder has always been a controversial film, but Ben Stiller has always been proud of it. It was a satirical look at method acting and actors who take themselves too seriously. Not only did Stiller star in the film, but he directed it as well. Most critics recognized that the blackface by Robert Downey Jr.'s character and the ableist portrayal by Stiller's character were done as a scathing commentary, and praised it for taking such risks.

There's Something About Mary (1998) â 84%

There's Something About Mary is one of those '90s movies that you remember being funny but are slightly horrified watching it today. A bunch of men obsessing over one woman (Cameron Diaz) was portrayed as a light-hearted romantic comedy, but it would be a horror film if made now. Regardless, Stiller's character is the most decent and does help protect Mary (Diaz) from stalkers and creeps. And critics have ranked this film as one of Stiller's best performances.

While We're Young (2014) â 84%

One of Stiller's more heartfelt comedies, While We're Young is about a couple's mid-life crisis. Stiller plays Josh Srebnick, a filmmaker looking to re-spark his life and his marriage. After meeting a fan of his films, Josh decides that he and his wife (Naomi Watts) should befriend the younger man (Adam Driver) and his wife (Amanda Seyfried). Cue all the tropes about trying to act cool to fit in with a younger generation, but in a way that the audience relates to and empathizes.

Meet the Parents (2000) â 85%

The first time Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro played opposite each other proved to be comedy gold. There is a reason that there are now four films in the series. In Meet the Parents, Stiller plays the unfortunately named Greg Focker, who plans to propose to his girlfriend (Teri Polo) after meeting her parents and getting her father's (De Niro) blessing. This movie should be considered a disaster movie from the amount of mishaps, but it is hilarious to see Greg continue to flounder.

Flirting With Disaster (1996) â 88%

Flirting With Disaster is a strange road trip comedy where Ben Stiller's character is searching for his biological parents. He and his wife, played by Patricia Arquette, decide to take a trip to meet his parents after a caseworker (TÃ©a Leoni) finds their names in the adoption agency database. For some reason, she joins the couple and flirts with Mel (Stiller), causing some obvious friction between him and his wife. Oh, and did we mention that the infant son that Mel refuses to name until he knows his "roots" is also along for the ride? Just a regular family trip!

The Meyerowitz Stories (New and Selected) (2017) â 92%

Stiller has demonstrated that family-centered comedies are his fortÃ©, and this holds true for his highest rated film, The Meyerowitz Stories. Starring alongside Adam Sandler, Dustin Hoffman, Elizabeth Marvel, and Emma Thompson, Stiller is a part of the dysfunctional Meyerowitz family. He plays the half-brother and favorite child, Matthew. This film shows Stiller's range and depth in both comedic and dramatic roles.
